title: Creatives that stay honest
summary: How to write, design and test sweeps creatives that make an honest prize promise: angles, formats, disclosures and real urgency without fake winners. You judge every creative on network-paid leads with written kill, hold and scale rules.

lessons.title: The honest prize promise
objectives: By the end you can name the six parts of an honest prize promise and spot the missing one in any ad.
By the end you can show with numbers why an honest promise often costs less per confirmed lead.
By the end you can check an ad and its lander against a promise checklist before launch.

steps.h: Why the promise decides your money
steps.p: In sweeps, the ad sells one thing: a fair chance at a prize in exchange for an email, a postcode or ZIP code, or a few answers. If the promise is honest, people confirm their entry and open the emails that follow. If it overpromises, ads are rejected, leads are scrubbed and complaints damage every send after.

d.b: Your ad is a promise. The lead pays you only if the promise holds.
d.s: Modules 1 to 3 covered the offer, the law and the funnel. This module is about the words and pictures.

steps.say: In sweeps, the ad sells one thing: a fair chance at a prize, in exchange for an email, a postcode or ZIP code, or a few answers. That's why the screen says your ad is a promise, and the lead pays you only if the promise holds. If the promise is honest, people confirm their entry and open the emails that follow. If it overpromises, ads get rejected, leads get scrubbed, and complaints damage every send after. Earlier modules covered the offer, the law and the funnel. This one is about the words and pictures.

steps.h: The six parts of an honest prize promise
steps.p: Every compliant sweeps creative answers six questions, either in the ad itself or one tap away on the lander. When one is missing, people fill the gap with their own guess, and their guess is usually bigger than the truth. That gap is where rejections and complaints start.
d: Prize|what it is, plus its approximate value
Chance|a chance to win, never a win
Exchange|what the entrant gives: email, ZIP, quiz
Deadline|the real closing date of the draw
Who can enter|country, age 18+, other limits
Rules|link to the official rules and sponsor name
steps.say: Every compliant sweeps creative answers six questions, either in the ad or one tap away on the lander. Look at the cards. The prize: what it is, and its approximate value. Chance: a chance to win, never a win. The exchange: what the entrant gives. The deadline: the real closing date. Who can enter: country, age eighteen plus, other limits. And the rules: a link to the official rules and the sponsor's name. When one is missing, people fill the gap with a guess that's usually bigger than the truth.

steps.p: The left column is copy we see in rejected sweeps ads. The right column says the same thing honestly. Notice that the honest version still names the prize clearly. Honest does not mean dull; it means a person who reads the ad knows exactly what happens when they tap.
steps.more: Free phone, just pay shipping is a classic card-submit trap: the shipping charge often starts a hidden subscription. Do not promote offers that work this way, even when the payout is high. They lead to chargebacks, regulator complaints and banned accounts, and some networks still list them.

a.title: Overpromise
items: Congratulations, you have won a phone

b.title: Honest promise
items: Enter for a chance to win a phone
Free to enter, no purchase necessary
Open to adults in South Africa

steps.say: Compare the two columns. On the left is copy we see in rejected sweeps ads: congratulations, you have won a phone. Only three prizes left. Free phone, just pay shipping. You have been selected. On the right, the honest versions: enter for a chance to win a phone. Draw closes thirty first October. Free to enter, no purchase necessary. Open to adults in South Africa. Notice the honest version still names the prize clearly. And watch out for free phone, just pay shipping. That shipping charge often starts a hidden subscription. Don't promote offers that work that way.

steps.p: Example. Ad A says you won. Ad B says enter for a chance. Ad A gets twice the clicks for the same spend, but people who expected a prize abandon the confirmation email. Per confirmed lead, the honest ad is cheaper, and that is before Ad A gets the account flagged.
steps.more: The maths: Ad A, $100 ÷ 90 = $1.11 per confirmed lead. Ad B, $100 ÷ 100 = $1.00. Ad A also sends 410 unconfirmed or angry entries into the advertiser's system, which raises the scrub rate on your whole account. In real life Ad A would likely be rejected before it spent $100, so this table is generous to it. All figures are an Example, not a benchmark.
steps.say: Here's an example. Two ads, one hundred dollars each. Ad A says you won. Ad B says enter for a chance. Read down the table. Ad A gets twice the clicks, one thousand two hundred and fifty against six hundred and twenty five, and more entries. But only eighteen percent confirm, against fifty percent for Ad B. So per confirmed lead, Ad A costs about one dollar eleven, and the honest Ad B costs one dollar. And in real life, Ad A would likely be rejected before it spent a hundred dollars. All figures are an example, not a benchmark.

steps.h: The number that matters in creative work
steps.p: Judge a sweeps creative on what you are paid for, not on clicks. If the offer pays per confirmed (DOI) lead, divide spend by confirmed leads. If it pays per accepted SOI lead, divide by accepted leads. A creative with a high click-through rate and a poor confirmation rate is a cost, not a winner.
d: Spend
Paid leads
Cost per paid lead
steps.say: Here's the number that matters in creative work. Follow the equation: spend, divided by paid leads, equals cost per paid lead. Judge a sweeps creative on what you're actually paid for, not on clicks. If the offer pays per confirmed lead, that's D O I, double opt-in, divide by confirmed leads. If it pays per accepted S O I, single opt-in, lead, divide by accepted leads. A creative with a high click-through rate but a poor confirmation rate is a cost, not a winner.

steps.h: Lab: the most you can pay per entry
steps.p: Example. The offer pays $1.50 per confirmed lead. Your honest ad gets 45% of entries to confirm. You want a 25% margin. Work out the most you can pay per submitted entry, then check. This is the line every creative in this module is judged against.
steps.more: $1.50 × 45% = $0.675 earned per submitted entry on average. Keep 25%: $0.675 × 0.75 = about $0.51. If your entries cost more than $0.51 each, you lose margin. If your confirmation rate drops to 18%, like Ad A, the same sum gives $1.50 × 18% × 0.75 = about $0.20 per entry. That is how a misleading hook quietly destroys the maths.

d.task: Payout $1.50 per confirmed lead, 45% of entries confirm, 25% margin. What is the most you can pay per submitted entry?

steps.say: Time for a lab. In this example, the offer pays one dollar fifty per confirmed lead. Your honest ad gets forty five percent of entries to confirm. And you want to keep a twenty five percent margin. Your task is to work out the most you can pay per submitted entry. Think about how much each entry earns on average, then how much of that you keep. This is the line every creative in this module is judged against. Pause and try it, then check your answer.

steps.h: The lander must say the same thing
steps.p: Message match: the first screen of the lander repeats the prize, the chance, the deadline and the rules link from the ad. If the ad says solar kit and the lander says win cash, people feel tricked and leave, and reviewers treat it as misleading. Module 3 covered lander structure; here we check the words.

page.p: Enter for a chance to win. Free entry, SA residents 18+. Draw closes 31 Oct. Read the official rules.

steps.say: The lander must say the same thing as the ad. That's message match. Look at the phone. The first screen repeats the prize, the five K V A solar inverter kit. It says enter for a chance to win, free entry, South African residents eighteen plus, the closing date of thirty first October, and links to the official rules. If the ad says solar kit and the lander says win cash, people feel tricked and leave, and reviewers treat it as misleading.

steps.p: Prize promotions fall under sweepstakes or competition law in most countries, and under platform rules on promotions and misleading claims. Your ad must match the official rules from Module 2 exactly: same prize, same dates, same eligibility. We are not certain the current wording of Meta's rules on prize promotions matches this summary; check Meta's Advertising Standards and Help Center before relying on it.

d.text: No implied wins, no hidden costs, no prize that differs from the rules. Check local law and the platform's current policy before every new promotion.

steps.say: Prize ads are regulated. Prize promotions fall under sweepstakes or competition law in most countries, and under platform rules on promotions and misleading claims. Your ad must match the official rules exactly: same prize, same dates, same eligibility. We're not certain the current wording of Meta's rules on prize promotions matches this summary, so check Meta's Advertising Standards and Help Center before relying on it. As the warning says: no implied wins, no hidden costs, and no prize that differs from the rules.

steps.p: Run this list on every ad and its lander before you publish. If any line fails, fix it first. It takes two minutes and prevents most rejections we see in sweeps accounts. Keep a copy in your launch sheet so your team uses the same list.
d: Prize named exactly as in the official rules
Says chance or enter, never won or selected
Real closing date shown on ad or lander
Country and age limits shown
Rules link and sponsor name on the lander
No cost or card needed to enter
steps.say: Run this promise checklist on every ad and its lander before you publish. Is the prize named exactly as in the official rules? Does it say chance or enter, never won or selected? Is the real closing date shown on the ad or lander? Are the country and age limits shown? Are the rules link and sponsor name on the lander? And is there no cost or card needed to enter? If any line fails, fix it first. It takes two minutes, and it prevents most of the rejections we see.

steps.p: These mistakes rarely come from bad intent. They come from copying what competitors run and from chasing click-through rate. Each one has a simple fix that keeps the ad honest and still clear about the prize.
d: Copying a rival's winning ad|write your own from the official rules
Prize value rounded up|use the value in the rules
Deadline left out|show the real closing date
Rules link only in the footer|link it near the entry button
Same ad after the draw closed|switch off or update on the end date
steps.say: These mistakes rarely come from bad intent. They come from copying competitors and chasing click-through rate. Look at the cards. Copying a rival's winning ad? Write your own from the official rules. Prize value rounded up? Use the value in the rules. Deadline left out? Show the real closing date. Rules link only in the footer? Put it near the entry button. Same ad running after the draw closed? Switch it off or update it on the end date.

steps.p: Starting rules to adapt to your offer and data. Apply them before launch and at the first read point. They protect your accounts and catch a weak promise before it eats budget.
steps.more: Why 0.6 × the network average: if the network says a typical confirmation rate on this offer is 40%, and yours is 24% or less after 100 entries, people are probably entering under a wrong impression. Ask the network for the average; if they do not have one, use your own best ad as the baseline. These are starting rules, not laws.

rows: Ad says won, winner or selected
Confirm rate below 0.6 × network average after 100 entries

steps.say: Here are starting decision rules for the promise. Read down the table. If the ad says won, winner or selected, don't launch. If the lander's prize differs from the ad, fix it before launch. If the confirm rate is below zero point six times the network average after one hundred entries, rewrite the promise or pause, because people are probably entering under a wrong impression. If an ad is rejected for misleading claims, rewrite it, and never resubmit it unchanged. And when the draw end date passes, switch off the same day.

steps.p: This is the chain we see when an ad oversells. Each step costs money or account health, and the last step can end the campaign entirely. Breaking the chain at the first step, the words in the ad, is far cheaper than fixing it later.
d: Click on a promise of a win
Entry with low intent
No confirmation, spam reports
Scrubs and lower payouts
Ad rejections or account limits
steps.say: Here's the chain we see when an ad oversells. Follow it along. A click on a promise of a win. An entry with low intent. No confirmation, and spam reports. Then scrubs and lower payouts. And finally, ad rejections or account limits, which can end the campaign entirely. Each step costs money or account health. Breaking the chain at the very first step, the words in the ad, is far cheaper than fixing it later.

options: You have won a solar kit
Claim your solar kit before it is gone
Enter for a chance to win a solar kit

quiz.why: Only enter for a chance describes the real situation; the others imply a win or false scarcity.

quiz.why: $100 ÷ 100 = $1.00 is lower than $100 ÷ 90 = $1.11; CTR does not change what you are paid for.

The ad says solar kit but the lander headline says win cash. What is the problem?
options: Nothing if the CTR is good
quiz.why: The lander must repeat the ad's promise; a different prize looks like a bait and switch.

quiz.why: 22% is below 0.6 × 40% = 24% after 100+ entries, which points to a misleading or unclear promise.

lessons.title: Angles and hooks that stay honest
objectives: By the end you can list five sweeps angles and say which offer type each fits.
By the end you can write three honest hooks for one angle.
By the end you can plan an angle test with a budget and a read point.

steps.h: Why the angle matters more than the picture
steps.p: The angle is the reason a person should care right now. Two ads with the same prize and the same picture can differ two or three times in cost per confirmed lead because one gives a better reason. Angles are also where most dishonest shortcuts creep in, so we learn both at once.

d.b: Angle = the reason to enter today
d.s: A hook is the first line or first second that delivers it.

steps.say: The angle is the reason a person should care right now. Two ads with the same prize and the same picture can differ two or three times in cost per confirmed lead, just because one gives a better reason. As the screen says, the angle is the reason to enter today, and the hook is the first line or first second that delivers it. Angles are also where most dishonest shortcuts creep in, so we'll learn both at once.

steps.p: These five cover most sweeps and lead gen offers. Each can be done honestly. Pick the angle that fits the offer: a single big prize suits the prize angle; a monthly draw suits the deadline angle; a sample or coupon offer suits the utility angle.
d: The prize|show it, its use, its value
The real deadline|when the draw actually closes
Local relevance|a prize that solves a local problem
Utility|samples, coupons, useful info for an email
Curiosity quiz|a short quiz that leads to the entry
steps.say: These five angles cover most sweeps and lead gen offers, and each one can be done honestly. Look at the cards. The prize: show it, its use and its value. The real deadline: when the draw actually closes. Local relevance: a prize that solves a local problem. Utility: samples, coupons or useful info in exchange for an email. And the curiosity quiz: a short quiz that leads to the entry. Pick the angle that fits the offer. A single big prize suits the prize angle, and a monthly draw suits the deadline angle.

steps.h: Match the angle to the offer type
steps.p: Different offer types pay for different actions, so the best angle differs. Module 1 explained SOI, DOI and ZIP submits. Here is how angle choice follows from them. Treat this as a starting map, then let your own data overrule it.
steps.say: Different offer types pay for different actions, so the best angle differs. Read across the table. If the offer pays for an S O I, single opt-in, email, start with prize or utility, because there's low friction and a clear exchange. For a D O I, double opt-in, confirmed email, start with prize or deadline, because people need intent to confirm. For a ZIP or short form, try local relevance or a quiz. And for a survey or quiz lead, a curiosity quiz matches the task. Treat this as a starting map, and let your own data overrule it.

steps.h: Same angle, dishonest versus honest hook
steps.p: Every angle has a dishonest version that clicks well for a week and then fails review or scrubs. The honest version still uses emotion and specifics. Read both columns aloud; if a hook would embarrass you in front of the sponsor, do not run it.

a.title: Dishonest hook
items: Last chance, ends in 10 minutes (it does not)

b.title: Honest hook
items: Power cuts again? Enter to win a solar kit
Answer 3 questions to enter the draw

steps.say: Every angle has a dishonest version that clicks well for a week, then fails review or gets scrubbed. Compare the columns. Last chance, ends in ten minutes, when it doesn't, becomes draw closes Friday at midnight. Thousands have already won becomes one winner drawn on thirty first October. An invented Lagos mum winning an inverter becomes power cuts again, enter to win a solar kit. And answer three questions to get paid becomes answer three questions to enter the draw. If a hook would embarrass you in front of the sponsor, don't run it.

steps.p: Example of a hook brief sent to a creator. One angle, local relevance, written three ways. Each hook says enter or chance, names the prize and fits the first two seconds of a video or the first line of a static ad.

1. Another power cut tonight? Enter to win a solar kit.
2. What would you run first with 5kVA of solar?
3. Free entry: one solar kit, drawn 31 Oct.

steps.say: Here's an example of a hook brief sent to a creator. One angle, power cuts, which is local relevance, written three ways. Read the chat. One: another power cut tonight, enter to win a solar kit. Two: what would you run first with five K V A of solar? Three: free entry, one solar kit, drawn thirty first October. Each hook says enter or chance, names the prize, and fits the first two seconds of a video or the first line of a static ad.

steps.p: Before you write hooks, look at which angles and formats other advertisers in your geo keep running for weeks. Use this to learn angles and gaps, never to copy someone's creative. Ad libraries show what is running, not what is profitable. Long-running is a hint, not proof.

steps.h: Walkthrough: research to brief in four steps
steps.p: This is a 30-minute routine before every new angle test. Tool screens are generic mock-ups; names change. The output is a one-page brief with three angles and three hooks each, written from the official rules.

steps.title: Read the rules
steps.text: Note the prize, value, deadline and eligibility. These are fixed facts every hook must respect.

blocks.label: Restrictions

steps.title: Scan running ads
steps.text: Filter by geo and keyword. Note angles, not wording. Mark ads that look misleading so you avoid them.

steps.title: Pick three angles
steps.text: One proven angle, one variation, one untested. Write why each fits the offer.

steps.title: Write three hooks each
steps.text: Run each hook against the promise checklist from Lesson 1 before it goes to design.

rows: Load shedding again? Enter to win solar
Win a solar kit worth R25,000
Which appliance would you power first?

steps.say: Here's a thirty minute routine before every new angle test. Tap Next to follow each step. One: read the rules. Note the prize, value, deadline and eligibility, plus restrictions like no implied wins and no brand logos. These are fixed facts every hook must respect. Two: scan running ads. Filter by geo and keyword, note angles, not wording, and mark misleading ads so you avoid them. Three: pick three angles, one proven, one variation, one untested, and write why each fits. Four: write three hooks for each, and run every hook against the promise checklist before it goes to design.

steps.p: Example from a $180 test, three angles at $60 each, offer paying $1.50 per confirmed lead with a $1.13 target. The quiz angle won on clicks but lost on confirmations. Load shedding won on the number that pays.
steps.more: Target: $1.50 × (1 − 25%) = $1.125, about $1.13. A1: $60 ÷ 68 = $0.88, under the 0.85 × scale line of $0.96. A2: $60 ÷ 44 = $1.36, above target but under the 1.3 × kill line ($1.47): hold and iterate the hook. A3: $60 ÷ 39 = $1.54, above $1.47, so kill. It had the most clicks and fewest confirms: its confirm rate per click is 7.5% against A1's 16.6%, a sign the quiz attracts players, not entrants. Example figures only.

steps.p: Local pain points such as power cuts or rising prices are fair angles when you state facts. Do not invent crises, use news of disasters to sell, or suggest the prize solves something it cannot. Do not target or imply personal hardship, which Meta and other platforms restrict. We are not certain of every current rule; check the platform's policy.

d.text: Use facts people already know. Never exploit fear, tragedy or personal financial hardship to get an entry.

steps.say: Local pain points, like power cuts or rising prices, are fair angles when you state facts. But don't invent crises, use news of disasters to sell, or suggest the prize solves something it can't. And don't target or imply personal hardship, which Meta and other platforms restrict. We're not certain of every current rule, so check the platform's policy. The warning sums it up: use facts people already know, and never exploit fear, tragedy or personal financial hardship to get an entry.

steps.p: Most failed angle tests failed because of the test, not the angles. These are the common errors we see in beginner angle tests and the simple fix for each one. Check your plan against them before launch.
d: Testing 10 angles on $50|test 3 angles with enough spend each
Changing picture and hook together|change one thing per test
Judging on CTR|judge on cost per paid lead
Copying competitor wording|copy nothing; learn the angle
Stopping on day one|wait for the read point
steps.say: Most failed angle tests failed because of the test, not the angles. Look at the cards. Testing ten angles on fifty dollars? Test three angles with enough spend each. Changing the picture and hook together? Change one thing per test. Judging on C T R, click-through rate? Judge on cost per paid lead. Copying competitor wording? Copy nothing, and learn the angle instead. Stopping on day one? Wait for the read point. Check your plan against these before launch.

steps.p: Starting rules to adapt. These match the rule card from Module 1: the minimum read is 20 × your target cost per confirmed lead. With a $1.13 target, that is about $23 per angle. Decide only then, on network-confirmed numbers.

rows: Hold; test new hooks on it
Keep; build more hooks on it
Rewrite: the hook draws the wrong people

steps.say: Here are the starting decision rules for angles. The minimum read is twenty times your target cost per confirmed lead, so about twenty three dollars per angle. Read down the table. Zero confirmed after five times target, about five sixty five: check tracking, then kill. Above one point three times target: kill the angle. Between target and one point three times: hold, and test new hooks on it. At or under zero point eight five times target with fifty plus confirmed: keep, and build more hooks. High C T R but a weak confirm rate: rewrite, because the hook draws the wrong people.

Research running angles
Pick 3 angles, write 3 hooks
Test at equal budget
Decide at the read point
steps.say: Here's the order to follow for every new offer. Follow the flow. Read the official rules. Research running angles. Pick three angles and write three hooks for each. Test them at equal budget. Then decide at the read point. The winning angle becomes the base for the format and copy work in the next lessons.

lessons.title: Testing creatives on paid leads
objectives: By the end you can set up a fair creative test for a sweeps offer.
By the end you can apply kill, hold and scale rules on cost per paid lead.

steps.h: Why the metric picks the winner
steps.p: A creative test is a small bet that tells you where to put the big money. If you judge on clicks, you will pick hooks that draw curious people who never confirm. If you judge on cost per paid lead, you pick ads that make money. The test budget is the same either way; only the decision differs.

d.s: Clicks and entries are clues, paid leads are the result.

steps.say: A creative test is a small bet that tells you where to put the big money. If you judge on clicks, you'll pick hooks that draw curious people who never confirm. Clicks and entries are clues, and paid leads are the result.

steps.h: Your target cost per paid lead
steps.p: Every rule in this lesson is built on one number: the target cost per paid lead. You get it from the payout and your margin. With $1.50 per confirmed lead and a 25% margin, the target is about $1.13. Use network-confirmed leads, not platform-reported ones.
steps.more: Example: $1.50 × 0.75 = $1.125, rounded to $1.13. Scale line: 0.85 × $1.13 = $0.96. CPL kill line: 1.3 × $1.13 = $1.47. Minimum read: 20 × $1.13 = about $23 of spend per ad set. Zero-lead kill: 0 paid leads after 5 × target, about $5.65. These are the Module 1 rule card lines; starting rules to adapt.

steps.say: Every rule in this lesson is built on one number: the target cost per paid lead. Follow the equation: payout, times one minus your margin, equals your target. With one dollar fifty per confirmed lead and a twenty five percent margin, the target is about one dollar thirteen. From that, the scale line is about ninety six cents, the kill line about one dollar forty seven, and the minimum read about twenty three dollars per ad set. Use network confirmed leads, not platform reported ones.

And a decision at the read point. In other words, change only one thing, the creative concept, then wait for the read point, and decide on network numbers. It's the structure from the operator school, applied to lead gen volumes.

steps.p: Starting rules to adapt, the same card as Module 1. Lead gen pays small amounts per lead, so you need more leads per decision than with FTD offers. The general calculator kills at 1.5 × target; for lead gen, apply the stricter 1.3 × line yourself. Use network-paid leads where you can; if they arrive late, use your validated leads and confirm later.

steps.say: The lead gen rules, with a one dollar thirteen target. Zero paid leads after five times target, about five sixty five of spend: kill. Minimum read is twenty times target, about twenty three dollars. After that, above one point three times target, over one forty seven: kill. Between one and one point three times: hold. At or under zero point eight five times target, ninety six cents, with fifty plus paid leads over three plus days: scale twenty percent every forty eight hours. Lead gen pays small amounts per lead, so you need more leads per decision. The general calculator kills at one point five times, so apply this stricter line yourself.

steps.p: Example over seven days for a winning ad. Frequency rises as the same people see it again, and cost per paid lead climbs with it. A starting rule: refresh when cost per paid lead rises 30% above its first-four-day average for 3 days in a row.
steps.more: First-four-day average cost: (0.85 + 0.86 + 0.90 + 0.98) ÷ 4 = about $0.90. 30% above is $1.17. By day 7 the ad is at $1.18, its first day above the line; if days 8 and 9 stay above $1.17, refresh. Have the next variations ready before this point, not after. Frequency figures are Example values; healthy levels vary by audience size and geo.
steps.say: Now, spotting fatigue. This chart is an example over seven days for a winning ad. Follow the two lines. Frequency rises from about one point two to three point five, as the same people see the ad again. And cost per paid lead climbs with it, from eighty five cents to about one dollar eighteen. A starting rule: refresh when cost per paid lead rises thirty percent above its first four day average for three days in a row. Here that average is about ninety cents, so the line is about one dollar seventeen, and day seven is the first day above it. Have your next variations ready before that point, not after.
